findings.title: Minimum token schema does not implement the intended permissive schema
findings.body: The two computed keys are both produced by calling toString() on Zod objects, so they collapse to the same property name ("[object Object]") instead of creating number/unknown catch-all entries. The resulting schema only retains access_token, and Zod strips the provider's other fields such as refresh_token, expires_in/expiry, scope and token_type. Callers that persist or spread the parsed data therefore lose the fields needed for subsequent refreshes.

findings.title: Helper injects the literal string "refresh_token" as a real refresh token
findings.body: When the parsed response has no refresh_token, the helper sets refresh_token to the literal placeholder "refresh_token". This is especially harmful in credential-sharing mode because the minimum schema strips any real refresh_token before this check. Callers that persist parsed data overwrite the stored provider refresh token with the placeholder, so later direct provider refreshes fail with an invalid grant.

findings.title: Credential-sync branch returns a different type from the normal refresh branch
findings.body: The normal branch returns whatever refreshFunction returns, which varies by caller: a Google response object with .data, a HubSpot SDK token object, or an Axios response with .data. The sync branch always returns a raw fetch Response, which has none of those shapes. Google then reads res.data.access_token, HubSpot reads expiresIn/accessToken, and the Zoho services read tokenInfo.data, so synced refreshes return undefined values, throw, or persist an unusable Response object instead of refreshed credentials.

findings.title: Google refresh stores the SafeParse wrapper object as the credential key
findings.body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod SafeParse result ({ success, data }), but this code assigns that whole result to `key` and writes it to prisma.credential. The stored key is therefore { success: true, data: {...credentials} } rather than the credential fields themselves. The next GoogleCalendarService construction calls googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key), which no longer matches, breaking the credential after the first token refresh even when credential sharing is disabled.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh uses prisma without importing it
findings.body: The newly added refresh block calls prisma.credential.update, but this file has no prisma import. Constructing the Salesforce service after a token refresh will fail type checking and, if emitted, throw a ReferenceError at runtime, breaking Salesforce event creation.

findings.title: Salesforce token schema requires fields Salesforce refresh responses do not return
findings.body: salesforceTokenSchema requires scope in addition to id, issued_at, instance_url, signature, access_token and token_type. Salesforce's refresh-token response normally returns access_token, instance_url, id, token_type, issued_at and signature, without scope. With credential sharing disabled parseRefreshTokenResponse uses this schema and throws, and with sharing enabled the minimum schema strips the fields anyway, so valid Salesforce refreshes are rejected.

findings.title: Salesforce client is built with the old access token after refreshing
findings.body: getClient fetches and stores a refreshed token, but constructs the jsforce Connection with accessToken: credentialKey.access_token, i.e. the expired token from the original credential, instead of accessTokenParsed.data.access_token. The API calls made through this connection will still use the stale token and fail authentication until some later construction happens to reload the credential.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin sends the credential ID as the Cal.com user ID to the sync endpoint
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens expects its third argument to be the credential owner's userId and sends it as calcomUserId, but this call passes credentialId (the credential row ID). The parent platform will look up the wrong user, fail to find tokens, or return another user's access token, which would then be stored under this credential and used for this user's Zoho Bigin account.

findings.title: Synced Office 365 refresh loses the expiry transform and overwrites the refresh token
findings.body: In sharing mode parseRefreshTokenResponse strips expires_in, so the refreshTokenResponseSchema transform that converts expires_in into an absolute expiry never runs, leaving the stored expiry in the past and forcing a refresh on every API call. The helper also adds the placeholder refresh_token, and the spread of tokenResponse.data overwrites the real stored Microsoft refresh token with that placeholder.

findings.title: Synced Zoom refresh persists a placeholder refresh token and NaN expiry
findings.body: In sharing mode the minimum schema strips expires_in and refresh_token from the sync endpoint response, then the helper inserts refresh_token: "refresh_token". This code assigns newTokens.refresh_token into the stored key and computes expiry_date from newTokens.expires_in, which is undefined, producing NaN. The persisted Zoom credential is corrupted and subsequent zoomTokenSchema parsing/refresh attempts fail.

findings.title: Webex synced refresh can never satisfy the refreshed-token schema
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens documents that the sync endpoint returns only an access token and expiry, but this code still validates the response with webexRefreshedTokenSchema, which requires the literal Webex scope, token_type Bearer, a real refresh_token and refresh_token_expires_in. A conforming sync-endpoint response is therefore always rejected with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned", so Webex token refresh does not work when credential sharing is enabled.

findings.title: Webhook handler has no error handling for malformed or undecryptable payloads
findings.body: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse, symmetricDecrypt and JSON.parse can all throw, and the handler has no try/catch or safeParse handling. An authenticated caller sending a malformed body, non-encrypted keys string, or non-JSON decrypted payload causes an unhandled exception and a 500 response instead of a controlled 400, making integration failures hard to diagnose and retry correctly.

findings.title: Credential create/update is a racy find-then-write with no uniqueness guard
findings.body: The handler does findFirst for (userId, appId) and then creates a credential if none is found. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user and app can both observe no credential and both insert one, creating duplicate credentials; later deliveries only update the first row found, leaving a stale duplicate that other findFirst-based code may pick up. The comment acknowledges upsert cannot be used, but no transaction or unique handling replaces it.

findings.title: Webhook secret is compared with a timing-unsafe string comparison
findings.body: The shared webhook secret that authorizes writing arbitrary user credentials is checked with !==, which short-circuits on the first differing character and can leak prefix information through response timing. This endpoint should compare the supplied header and CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET with a constant-time comparison such as crypto.timingSafeEqual (with length handling).

findings.title: New credential-writing webhook and token-sync helpers have no tests
findings.body: This PR adds a security-sensitive endpoint that authenticates by shared secret, decrypts payloads and creates/updates stored OAuth credentials, plus token-refresh helpers used by many integrations, but adds no tests (the PR checklist also states tests were not added). There is no coverage proving disabled-sharing rejection, wrong-secret rejection, decrypt/create/update behavior, or that synced refresh responses preserve expiry and refresh tokens for each provider shape, which is how the return-shape and field-stripping regressions above shipped unnoticed.
